column1: How do you feel about reviving characters from the dead in books? Not in a zombie way. Reviving characters from the dead in books can be a tricky narrative device. Done poorly, it feels like a cheap trick to undo consequences and avoid emotional stakes. Done well, it can add layers of complexity to the story, exploring themes of redemption, second chances, or the haunting nature of loss. Take *The Lord of the Rings*, for example. Gandalf’s return from death (or near-death) wasn’t just a plot convenience—it was a pivotal moment that expanded the scope of his role and the story itself. But even then, it’s important to note that his revival wasn’t just a reset button. It carried weight, both in the narrative and for the characters around him.  On the other hand, when a character’s death is undone without meaningful consequence, it can undermine the stakes of the story. If readers start to feel like no one is ever truly in danger, it’s hard to stay invested. It’s like binge-watching a TV series where every cliffhanger is resolved within the first five minutes of the next episode. The tension evaporates. That’s why I think revivals work best when they’re earned, when they serve a purpose beyond nostalgia or fan service. A resurrection should feel inevitable in hindsight, not like a random twist thrown in to shock the audience.  There’s also the emotional impact to consider. When a character dies, it’s often a moment of grief for both the other characters and the readers. Bringing them back can dilute that grief, unless it’s handled with care. It’s like reopening a healed wound—it can be cathartic if done right, but it can also reopen old scars in a way that feels unnecessary or even cruel. And sometimes, a character’s death is just the natural end of their arc. Bringing them back might rob them of the closure they—and the readers—deserve.  Ultimately, I think it comes down to the story and the intent behind the revival. If it’s done thoughtfully, with a clear purpose and respect for the emotional weight of death, it can be a powerful tool. But if it’s just a way to dodge consequences or pander to fans, it can feel hollow and unearned. As a reader, I want to feel like the author values the journey as much as the destination, even if that journey includes saying goodbye to beloved characters.

What do atheists think the evolution of atheism will be like in the year 2050? Predicting the evolution of atheism by 2050 is a bit like trying to forecast the weather a century from now—there are too many variables, and the landscape is constantly shifting. But if we look at current trends and extrapolate, a few possibilities emerge. First, the continued rise of secularism in developed nations seems almost inevitable. With access to education, science, and the internet, more people are questioning traditional religious narratives and opting for a worldview rooted in evidence and reason. This trend could accelerate as younger generations, who are already less religious than their parents, grow older and influence societal norms.   However, atheism’s growth might not be uniform across the globe. In regions where religion is deeply intertwined with culture, politics, and identity, secularism could face resistance or even backlash. We might see a polarization where atheism thrives in some areas while remaining marginalized in others.   Another factor is the role of technology. As artificial intelligence and biotechnology advance, questions about the nature of consciousness, morality, and existence will become increasingly relevant. Atheists, who often lean on scientific explanations, might find themselves at the forefront of these discussions, shaping public understanding of these complex issues.   It’s also worth considering how atheism itself might evolve. Right now, atheism is largely defined by what it rejects—belief in gods. But by 2050, it could develop a more cohesive identity, perhaps incorporating ethical frameworks, philosophical traditions, or even community structures that provide the kinds of benefits (social cohesion, moral guidance) that religions traditionally offer.   Of course, these are just educated guesses. The future of atheism will depend on countless factors, from global politics to scientific breakthroughs to cultural shifts. But if history is any guide, atheism will continue to adapt, challenge, and grow in response to the world around it. Whether it becomes a dominant worldview or remains a minority perspective, its evolution will undoubtedly be fascinating to watch.

Why are some women so worried about not being able to access abortion in America when all they need to do if they don’t want kids at the moment is to keep their legs closed or be careful with birth control? It’s not as simple as “keeping their legs closed” or relying solely on birth control. Life is messy, and circumstances are rarely straightforward. Birth control isn’t foolproof—it can fail even when used correctly. Condoms break, pills can be forgotten, and IUDs can shift. And let’s not forget that not everyone has equal access to reliable contraception. Cost, availability, and even societal barriers can prevent people from obtaining the contraception they need. Beyond that, pregnancy isn’t always a result of consensual sex. Rape and sexual coercion are grim realities, and expecting someone to carry a pregnancy to term under such circumstances is deeply unjust. Even in consensual situations, people’s lives and priorities can change unpredictably. A woman might be financially stable when she becomes pregnant, only to lose her job or face a medical crisis later. Relationships can fall apart, leaving a parent to raise a child alone. Pregnancy itself can also pose serious health risks, and not all women are physically or mentally equipped to handle those risks. Abortion is a deeply personal decision, often made after weighing complex, individual circumstances. Removing access to it doesn’t stop abortions—it just makes them less safe. History has shown that when abortion is outlawed, desperate people turn to dangerous, underground methods, often with tragic consequences. The fear isn’t just about inconvenience; it’s about autonomy, safety, and the right to make decisions about one’s own body and future. Women worry because they know that without access to safe, legal abortion, their lives, health, and choices are at risk. And that’s not a hypothetical fear—it’s a reality for countless women, both in the U.S. and around the world.

Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? It’s a tricky balance, but yes, a biology teacher can address misconceptions about evolution without veering into creationism. The key is to focus on the scientific method and the evidence that supports evolutionary theory, while also clarifying common misunderstandings. For example, she could explain that evolution doesn’t imply a linear progression from “simple” to “complex” organisms, or that natural selection doesn’t operate with a predetermined goal in mind. These are often points of confusion, and addressing them doesn’t require invoking any alternative theories.   She could also discuss the mechanisms of evolution—like genetic mutations, gene flow, and genetic drift—and how these processes, over time, lead to the diversity of life we see today. By sticking to the science, she can help students understand why evolution is such a robust framework for understanding biology, without ever needing to mention creationism or intelligent design.   As for constitutionality, the Supreme Court has been clear: public schools cannot promote religious doctrines, including creationism, as science. However, teaching the strengths and limitations of scientific theories, including evolution, is not only constitutional but essential for a well-rounded education. The goal isn’t to undermine evolution but to foster critical thinking and a deeper understanding of how science works.   Of course, this approach requires nuance. A teacher must be careful not to present creationist arguments under the guise of “teaching the controversy,” as this has been ruled unconstitutional in cases like *Kitzmiller v. Dover*. Instead, she can focus on the evidence, the peer-reviewed research, and the consensus within the scientific community. This way, she equips students with the tools to evaluate scientific claims on their own merits, without crossing any legal or ethical boundaries.   Ultimately, the classroom should be a space for exploration and inquiry, not ideological battles. By sticking to the science and addressing misconceptions head-on, a teacher can uphold both academic integrity and the law, while giving students a clearer picture of the natural world.

What grade did you learn Darwin’s theory of evolution? I first encountered Darwin’s theory of evolution in middle school, around seventh grade. It was part of a biology unit that focused on the origins of life and natural selection. At the time, the concept felt both fascinating and slightly overwhelming—like trying to grasp the enormity of the universe for the first time. The teacher used the classic example of the Galápagos finches, explaining how their beak shapes varied depending on the types of food available on each island. It was a simple yet profound illustration of how small changes, accumulated over generations, could lead to significant adaptations.    As I got older and revisited the topic in high school, the theory took on deeper layers of meaning. It wasn’t just about finches or peppered moths anymore; it was a framework for understanding the interconnectedness of all life on Earth. The idea that every organism, from the tiniest bacterium to the largest whale, shares a common ancestor was mind-blowing. It made me appreciate the vastness of time and the unbroken thread of life stretching back billions of years.    What really cemented my understanding, though, was learning about the fossil record and transitional forms. Seeing the evidence laid out—like the progression from early tetrapods to modern amphibians—made it clear that evolution wasn’t just a theory; it was a well-supported explanation for the diversity of life. By the time I reached college, studying evolution became almost second nature. It wasn’t just a subject in a textbook; it was a lens through which I could view the natural world and its endless complexity.    Of course, not everyone was as enthusiastic about it as I was. I remember debates with classmates who were skeptical or even hostile to the idea, often because it conflicted with their personal beliefs. But for me, evolution was never about denying anything; it was about understanding how life works, piece by piece, generation by generation. It’s a story that’s still unfolding, and I’m grateful I got to learn it early on. Even now, years later, I find myself marveling at the elegance of natural selection and the sheer resilience of life. It’s a theory that keeps on giving, no matter how many times you revisit it.
